```{r appendix-tier2}
               "selection mass, true mean below floor"),
  predicted_M18 = round(pred, 3), measured = measd),
  caption = sprintf(
    "Fixed-family benchmark (M = %d, floor 60/700) vs the measured n = 700 record.", M7))
top7 <- order(-sel)[1:3]
cat(sprintf("Top predicted selections: %s\n",
    paste(sprintf("%s %.3f", lab7[top7], sel[top7]), collapse = " | ")))
```

Reading the comparison, row by row, with each residual assigned to its
rung. **Detection** ($0.978$ predicted vs $0.999$): the real family is
far larger; more candidates raise the family exceedance — the stated
Level 5 direction. **Winner size and sensitivity** ($163$ vs $74$;
$0.287$ vs $0.123$): the regenerated family's fine cuts supply many small
candidates, and the noise-seeking argmax takes them — the scenario's own
signature of this regime appears in its top predicted selections, where
at the $8.6\%$ floor a **zero-purity** rule leads. **PPV** ($0.312$
predicted vs $0.402$ measured) is the honest miss in direction: the real
family's fine cuts also supply small *high-purity* slices of $Q$ that the
coarse $M = 18$ scenario cannot represent, so measured purity beats the
scenario ceiling — a regeneration effect with the opposite sign to the
sensitivity one, and a caution against reading the scenario's
classification rows as bounds. **E[$\beta(\hat H)$]** ($30.55$ vs
$31.76$) is near-quantitative, for a reason the locks make plain: the
quantity is pinned by the mixture identity to mean purity, and selection
concentrates just above the floor in both worlds. **Naive bias** ($+29.7$
vs $+77.1$): regeneration multiplies the winner's curse roughly
$2.6\times$ here — the direction stated in Step 4, its magnitude the
clearest single measure of what the fixed family cannot supply. The
predicted below-floor selection mass ($0.544$) has no directly tabulated
counterpart; its per-replicate analogue (share of detected replicates
with $\beta(\hat H) < c_1$) is computable from the bundle and is a
natural addition to the report.

## Tier 3 and the boundary

The replicate-faithful route of the worked example's final step — feeding
each replicate's realized family (candidate memberships and arm counts
from the fitted objects) into the design-conditional law — would replace
every Tier 2 attribution above with a measured decomposition: computed
detection, selection, and naive-bias per replicate, exact up to the gate
idealization and quadrature. It has not yet been executed; it is a
consumer of existing bundle objects. What no tier predicts, by
construction, is the MR correction's own residual: the measured $+22.17$
bias and $144.49$ mean width are inputs to the coverage composition
above, not outputs of the analytic layer — the empirical core the
simulations exist to measure, scored against references the certified
layer supplies exactly.

# Appendix B — Causal-inference reference results (Wager) {#sec-refwager}

This appendix makes the document self-contained on its causal-inference
foundations by restating, in this document's notation and with precise
citations, the results it uses or parallels from Stefan Wager's *Causal
Inference: A Statistical Learning Approach* (Stanford; draft dated
November 26, 2025), cited throughout as **[W]** with the draft's equation
and theorem numbers, and its ancestor, the STATS 361 lecture notes
(Spring 2020), cited as **[W-notes]**. Because [W] is a dated draft,
numbering may shift in print; the cited section titles are stable. Each
subsection ends with the role the result plays here.

## Potential outcomes, randomization, and difference in means {#sec-refwager-rct}

**Setup ([W] §1.1).** Each unit carries potential outcomes
$(Y_i(0), Y_i(1))$. SUTVA (eq. 1.5) states $Y_i = Y_i(W_i)$: the
observed outcome is the potential outcome of the assigned arm, with no
interference across units. Randomization (eq. 1.6) states that,
conditionally on all potential outcomes and on the treated count $n_1$,
every unit is treated with the same probability $n_1/n$. The
difference-in-means estimator (eq. 1.4) is
$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}} = n_1^{-1}\sum_{W_i=1} Y_i -
n_0^{-1}\sum_{W_i=0} Y_i$.

**Theorem 1.1 ([W]).** Under SUTVA and randomization,
$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}$ is finite-sample unbiased for the sample
average treatment effect, conditionally on the potential outcomes and on
both arms being non-empty. The proof is iterated expectation:
assignment independence pulls through the sum.

**Superpopulation CLT and the Neyman variance ([W] §1.1, around
eqs. 1.9–1.10).** With units i.i.d. from a population and treated
fraction $\pi_{\mathrm{tr}}$, define residuals
$\varepsilon_i(w) = Y_i(w) - \mathbb E[Y_i(w)]$. The estimation error
decomposes as
$$
\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}} - \tau
= \frac{n}{n_1}\cdot\frac1n\sum_i W_i\,\varepsilon_i(1)
- \frac{n}{n_0}\cdot\frac1n\sum_i (1-W_i)\,\varepsilon_i(0);
$$
the two per-arm sums are uncorrelated with variances
$\pi_{\mathrm{tr}}\,\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon(1)]$ and
$(1-\pi_{\mathrm{tr}})\,\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon(0)]$, and the CLT gives
$\sqrt n\,(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}} - \tau) \Rightarrow
N(0, V_{\mathrm{DM}})$ with
$$
V_{\mathrm{DM}}
= \frac{\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon(1)]}{\pi_{\mathrm{tr}}}
+ \frac{\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon(0)]}{1-\pi_{\mathrm{tr}}},
$$
consistently estimable by the arm-wise plug-in
$\widehat V_{\mathrm{DM}}$.

**Role here.** The §2 estimator is exactly this object restricted to a
region ($\pi_{\mathrm{tr}} = 1/2$); Proposition 1's Step 2 is eq. 1.6
surviving the conditioning on $\{X \in H\}$; the residual decomposition
is the seed of the influence representation $\psi_i(g)$ of
@sec-additive; the Neyman variance restricted to $g$ **is** the Level 4
diagonal (the identity displayed in @sec-ladder, Level 4); and the
consistent variance estimator is the ancestor of the Level 3 plug-in
observation.

## Regression adjustment in randomized trials {#sec-refwager-adj}

**[W] §1.2.** Adjusting the difference in means by fitted per-arm
outcome models leaves the estimator consistent under randomization
regardless of model quality, and reduces the asymptotic variance by the
portion of $\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon(w)]$ explained by the covariates —
the prognostic component. **Role here.** This is the population
statement of two facts the ladder measures: the per-region `lm` residual
variance absorbing within-region prognostic and CATE spread (inflation
factors $0.94$–$1.09$, Level 3), and the $u^{(g)}$ prognostic terms of
the additive decomposition (Level 4) being exactly the component an
adjusted estimator could remove — quantified as
$\mathrm{Var}(2\mu_0 + \tau \mid g)$ in the Level 4 identity.

## AIPW, the efficient influence function, and the efficiency bound {#sec-refwager-eff}

**AIPW ([W] §3.1–3.2).** Under unconfoundedness with propensity $e(x)$
and outcome regressions $\mu_{(w)}(x)$, the augmented IPW estimator
averages the scores
$$
\Gamma_i = \mu_{(1)}(X_i) - \mu_{(0)}(X_i)
+ \frac{W_i\,\big(Y_i - \mu_{(1)}(X_i)\big)}{e(X_i)}
- \frac{(1-W_i)\,\big(Y_i - \mu_{(0)}(X_i)\big)}{1 - e(X_i)}.
$$
**Theorem 3.2 ([W]), with cross-fitting:** with nuisances estimated at
$o(n^{-1/4})$ rates on held-out folds,
$\sqrt n\,(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{AIPW}} - \tau) \Rightarrow N(0, V^\ast)$
and the plug-in variance is consistent. **The bound (eq. 3.20) and
Theorem 3.4 ([W]):**
$$
V^\ast = \mathrm{Var}[\tau(X)]
+ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\sigma^2_{(1)}(X)}{e(X)}\right]
+ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\sigma^2_{(0)}(X)}{1-e(X)}\right]
$$
is the *efficient* variance in the local asymptotic minimax sense of
Hájek [1972], via the argument of Chamberlain [1992]: no estimator
improves on it uniformly over a neighborhood of any $P$.

**Role here.** Three uses. (i) Specialized to the fixture ($e = 1/2$,
homoscedastic noise) within a region,
$V^\ast(g) = 4\sigma^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\tau \mid g)$, and the Level 4
identity gives the exact excess of the package's unadjusted estimator
over the bound — $\mathrm{Var}(2\mu_0 + \tau \mid g)$, the adjustable
prognostic component (display in @sec-ladder, Level 4). (ii) The score
$\Gamma_i$, restricted to a region with known $e = 1/2$ and the
regression pieces absorbed into the centering, reduces to the
$\psi_i(g)$ of @sec-additive up to the $2/(nP(g))$ normalization; the
Gram/PSD structure of $\Sigma_{\mathrm{pop}}$ is the second-moment
structure of these scores. (iii) The Crump machinery's
`sandwich_var_glm` (the B2 and survival lanes of the detection-theory
NOTEs) is the empirical second moment of the same estimating-equation
scores at the basis level — the Level 3 plug-in layer, pre-built.

## The CATE, the R-learner frame, and the GRF identifier's target {#sec-refwager-cate}

**[W] §4.1–4.2.** The estimand is the conditional average treatment
effect $\tau(x) = \mu_{(1)}(x) - \mu_{(0)}(x)$. Estimating the two arm
surfaces separately and differencing incurs *regularization bias* — the
fits regularize differently and the difference inherits artifacts ([W]
Fig. 4.1: an oscillatory control fit against a flat treated fit
manufactures a spurious oscillatory CATE). The remedy targets $\tau$
directly: the semiparametric specification $\tau(x) = \psi(x)\cdot\beta$
with residual-on-residual regression, generalized in §4.2 to a loss
function for treatment heterogeneity whose minimization over flexible
classes defines the R-learner; the causal forest of Athey, Tibshirani,
and Wager [2019] instantiates this framework with random forests.

**Role here.** The GRF identifier's nominations target exactly this
$\tau(\cdot)$; Proposition 1 is the identity-scale collapsibility that
turns region means into linear functionals of $\tau$; and the fixture's
two-valued $\tau$ is the piecewise-constant case in which thresholding
rules are the natural optimal policies — the hinge to the next
subsection. Nomination itself remains unmodeled in the ladder (Level 5);
this subsection supplies its formal reference, not its law.

## Policy learning, empirical welfare maximization, and regret {#sec-refwager-policy}

**[W] §5.1–5.2.** A policy $\pi: x \mapsto \{0, 1\}$ has value
$V(\pi)$; with a test set under unconfoundedness, $V(\pi)$ is estimable
by IPW or AIPW value estimators (§5.1). Learning constrains $\pi$ to a
class $\Pi$ (linear thresholds, fixed-depth trees, …); the optimum is
$\pi^\ast \in \arg\max\{V(\pi'): \pi' \in \Pi\}$ (eq. 5.14), the regret
of any acceptable $\pi$ is
$R(\pi) = \sup_{\pi'} V(\pi') - V(\pi)$ (eq. 5.15), and
empirical-welfare maximization [Kitagawa and Tetenov, 2018] learns
$\hat\pi = \arg\max\{\widehat V(\pi): \pi \in \Pi\}$ (eq. 5.16). The
regret of EWM scales with the square root of the policy-class
complexity over $n$ ([W] §5.2, regret-bounds sketch), and the learning
problem reduces to weighted classification.

**Role here — kinship and contrast, with estimand discipline.** The
selection layer of this document and EWM are two lenses on one object:
an argmax over a rule class driven by noisy per-rule evaluations. The
kinships are exact in kind: the policy-class complexity term is the
bound-side face of what $L_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and the family joint law
measure on the exact-law side, and the winner's-curse functional (the
computed naive bias) is the finite-$n$ distributional content that
regret bounds envelope in expectation. The contrasts matter equally:
EWM targets the *value* $V(\pi)$ — a size-weighted welfare — with
guarantees over $\Pi$; this document's procedure ranks by the
*per-rule effect* under screening and consistency gates (maxeffCons is
argmax of effect among gate-passers, not argmax of welfare), and its
analytic layer computes the exact finite-$n$ law of that specific
procedure, targeting $\beta(\hat H)$. Neither subsumes the other: the
regret frame answers "how good a policy can learning guarantee"; the
present frame answers "what will this identifier do, with what
probabilities, on this design."

## Source map and scope

[W-notes] chapters 1–4 (RCTs; unconfoundedness; AIPW; heterogeneity)
are the ancestors of [W] chapters 1–4, and [W] Ch. 5 extends the
corresponding policy-learning lecture. Chapters of [W] beyond these —
balancing estimators, regression discontinuity, instruments and LATE,
interference, event studies, dynamic policies — are not used by this
document and are named only to delimit scope. Full bibliographic
entries for the works cited inside the restatements (Hájek 1972;
Chamberlain 1992; Kitagawa and Tetenov 2018; Athey, Tibshirani, and
Wager 2019) appear in [W]'s bibliography.
